title: Complementary Probability
coreInsight: Probability inherits complementary counting: an event and its complement exhaust the sample space, so their probabilities add to 1.
targetLearnerRealization: Complementary probability is the same complement idea from counting: an event and its opposite exhaust the sample space, so their probabilities sum to 1.
learningObjectives: Identify the exact complement of an event and verify that the two events cover the sample space without overlap.
Calculate a probability by subtracting the probability of its complement from 1.
Use complementary probability to solve at-least-one and other awkward event conditions.

continuity.openingCallback: Reuse C5's whole-minus-opposite check, then replace the counting whole with probability 1.
closingSeeds: A trustworthy complement must cover every possibility outside the event and none inside it.
Several awkward success cases may collapse into one simple failure event.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Subtracting one bad outcome is the same as subtracting the full complement.
An event and the proposed complement may fail to exhaust the sample space.
The complement rule is unrelated to earlier counting ideas.

beats.purpose: Briefly reactivate C5's exact-opposite move in the probability setting without naming a new rule.
beats.expectedRealization: The exact opposite of green is yellow or red, not merely one non-green color.
beats.transitionIn: C5 ended with a question: if the opposite chance is easier, what plays the role of the whole? Start with the familiar move—name the complete opposite.
beats.prompt: A 60-second light cycle is green for 25 seconds, yellow for 5, and red for 30. What is the exact opposite of “the light is green”?

visual.ariaLabel: A traffic-light cycle with green, yellow, and red durations listed neutrally

feedback.yellow: Red times are also not green, so yellow alone leaves part of the opposite behind.
feedback.red: Yellow times are also not green, so red alone leaves part of the opposite behind.
feedback.both: Yes—every non-green instant is yellow or red.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—yellow or red is the complete opposite event.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The opposite must contain every instant when green is false.

visual.ariaLabel: The completed split between green and not green, with yellow and red grouped as not green

steps.title: Negate the whole condition
steps.body: Not green includes both other colors: yellow or red.

resolution.takeaway: A complement is the entire other side, not just one unfavorable case.

beats.purpose: Make the learner establish coverage and non-overlap before using subtraction.
beats.expectedRealization: Green and not green are disjoint and together fill all 60 seconds; equal sizes are unnecessary.
beats.transitionIn: Naming the other side is not enough. C5's subtraction worked only because the two sides formed an exact partition.
beats.prompt: Which facts make “green” and “not green” a trustworthy two-part split? Select all that apply.

options.text: Together they cover every instant of the cycle.
No instant belongs to both events.
The two events last the same number of seconds.

response.feedback: A partition needs complete coverage and no overlap; its two parts do not need equal sizes.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—every instant is in exactly one of the two events.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Check two separate conditions: nothing is missed, and nothing is counted twice.

visual.ariaLabel: Green and not-green durations form the complete 60-second cycle

steps.title: Check coverage
steps.body: Green plus yellow plus red accounts for all 60 seconds.

steps.title: Check overlap
steps.body: At one instant, the light cannot be both green and not green.

resolution.takeaway: An event and its complement place every outcome on exactly one side.

beats.purpose: Use the approved visual anchor to turn complementary counting into subtraction from probability 1.
beats.expectedRealization: The full cycle has probability 1, so P(not green)=1-P(green)=1-25/60=7/12.
beats.transitionIn: The cycle is partitioned. Now decide what number represents the probability of that complete 60-second whole.
beats.transitionOut: C5 wrote whole minus opposite in counts. Here the probability whole was 1.
beats.whyNow: The learner has identified and audited the exact complement, so the mapped traffic-light problem can reveal that complementary probabilities partition 1.
beats.entryBridge: Use green as the easier side, then subtract its share of the cycle from the whole probability.
beats.exitBridge: Green contributes 25/60, so the complete other side contributes 1-25/60=35/60=7/12.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The same complete traffic cycle is partitioned into green and not-green regions.
learnerPrompts: What is the probability of the complete cycle?
What fraction of the cycle is green?
Why does subtracting that fraction leave every and only non-green instant?
beats.incorrectFeedback: The full probability is 1. Remove the 25/60 green part, not just one non-green color.

steps.title: Measure the easier event
steps.body: Green occupies 25 of the 60 equally likely instants in a cycle.

steps.title: Use the complete probability whole
steps.body: Green and not green fill the cycle without overlap, so their probabilities add to 1.

steps.title: Subtract
steps.body: Removing the green share leaves all 35 non-green seconds.

resolution.takeaway: Whole minus opposite survives unchanged; in probability, the complete whole is 1.

beats.purpose: Attach formal language and notation only after the learner has constructed the partition and subtraction.
beats.expectedRealization: An event E and its complement not E are disjoint, exhaustive, and have probabilities summing to 1.
beats.transitionIn: You already used the probability version of C5's move. Now name the exact-other-side relationship that made it legal.
beats.transitionOut: The formula is short, but its real work is naming the complete opposite correctly.
beats.name: Complementary probability
beats.conciseDefinition: The complement of an event E, written not E, contains every outcome where E does not occur and no outcome where E does occur.

beats.purpose: Repair common language errors by making the learner construct complete complements before calculating.
beats.expectedRealization: The complement of exactly one success includes both zero successes and at least two successes.
beats.transitionIn: Before using the formula again, test the part that carries the reasoning: translating a phrase into its entire opposite.
beats.prompt: Sort each event with its exact complement.

items.text: At least one head in three tosses
Exactly one head in three tosses

buckets.text: Zero heads or at least two heads

response.feedback: Negate the whole condition. Then test whether the pair covers every possibility exactly once.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—each pair covers all possibilities with no overlap.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Pay special attention to “exactly one”: its failure includes too few and too many, not only none.

groups.label: Exactly one head
choices: opposite: zero heads or at least two heads

visual.ariaLabel: Completed matching of three events with their exact complements

steps.title: Negate “at least one”
steps.body: It fails only when the count is zero.

steps.title: Negate “exactly one”
steps.body: It fails when the count is zero, two, or three.

resolution.takeaway: A complement contains every way the original condition can fail.

beats.purpose: Give a small, inspectable first use of subtracting an easier probability from 1.
beats.expectedRealization: Among 1 through 10, the four primes form the complement of not prime, so the desired probability is 1-4/10=3/5.
beats.transitionIn: Start with a one-step sample space where you can audit both sides by inspection.
beats.transitionOut: Subtracting the complete prime set—not one prime—left six non-prime cards.
beats.whyNow: The learner can focus on complement language and the probability whole before moving to repeated trials.
beats.entryBridge: List the prime cards as the complete opposite of the requested event.
beats.exitBridge: Four of ten cards are prime, so the other six of ten are not prime.
learnerPrompts: Which numbers from 1 through 10 are prime?
Does that list include every way for “not prime” to fail?
beats.incorrectFeedback: The prime cards are 2, 3, 5, and 7. Subtract all four from the ten-card whole.

visual.ariaLabel: Cards one through ten with the six non-prime cards marked

steps.title: Count the opposite
steps.body: The prime cards are 2, 3, 5, and 7.

steps.title: Subtract from the probability whole
steps.body: Every card is either prime or not prime.

resolution.takeaway: Subtract the probability of the complete opposite event from 1.

beats.purpose: Apply the complement rule to an at-least-one event with a single simple failure outcome.
beats.expectedRealization: At least one tail fails only at HHH, so its probability is 1-1/8=7/8.
beats.transitionIn: Now the desired event spreads across many coin outcomes. Look for the one way it fails.
beats.transitionOut: Seven success patterns collapsed into the single opposite pattern HHH.
beats.whyNow: This is the canonical near transfer from complementary counting to complementary probability.
beats.entryBridge: Translate “at least one tail” into the exact opposite before counting anything.
beats.exitBridge: Only HHH has no tails, so every other outcome belongs to the target event.
learnerPrompts: What is the exact opposite of at least one tail?
How many of the eight equally likely outcomes are on that opposite side?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—the complement HHH has probability 1/8, leaving 7/8.
beats.incorrectFeedback: At least one tail fails only if every toss is a head.

steps.title: Name the complete opposite
steps.body: At least one tail fails only when there are no tails: HHH.

steps.title: Measure and subtract
steps.body: Three fair tosses have eight equally likely outcomes, and HHH is one of them.

resolution.takeaway: At-least-one events often have a one-pattern complement: none.

beats.purpose: Prepare the mapped dice transfer by checking the number-theoretic event translation without revealing its probability.
beats.expectedRealization: With standard dice, a product is a multiple of 5 exactly when at least one die is 5, so the complement is neither die is 5.
beats.transitionIn: The coin complement was one outcome. On a dice grid, the simpler opposite will be a whole rectangle.
beats.prompt: For two standard dice, what is the exact opposite of “the product is a multiple of 5”?

feedback.no-double: If one die is 5 and the other is not, the product is still a multiple of 5.
feedback.neither: Yes—with faces 1 through 6, a product has a factor of 5 exactly when a die shows 5.
feedback.one: The original event also includes double 5, so exactly one 5 is not its opposite.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—the complete failure event is no 5 on either die.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Test (5,2) and (5,5). Both make multiples of 5, so the opposite must exclude every 5.

steps.title: Translate the product condition
steps.body: Among die faces 1 through 6, only 5 supplies a factor of 5.

steps.title: Negate “at least one”
steps.body: The exact opposite of at least one 5 is no 5 on either die.

resolution.takeaway: The complement is neither die shows 5—not merely “not both are 5.”

beats.purpose: Transfer complementary probability to a two-dimensional outcome space and expose the overlap trap in direct counting.
beats.expectedRealization: The 25 no-5 outcomes form the complement, so the desired probability is 1-25/36=11/36.
beats.transitionIn: You have named the no-5 rectangle. Use it to solve the full contest problem before inspecting the tempting overlapping row-and-column count.
beats.transitionOut: Complementary probability counted the clean 5 by 5 failure block and avoided repairing an overlapping success count.
beats.whyNow: The approved transfer problem replaces a timeline with a less obvious 6 by 6 sample space and tests whether the learner can find the complete complement independently.
beats.entryBridge: Give each die the five non-5 choices and compare that clean block with all 36 ordered outcomes.
beats.exitBridge: The no-5 block has 25 outcomes, leaving 11 of 36 with at least one 5.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A complete sample-space grid partitioned into the no-5 rectangle and its L-shaped complement.
learnerPrompts: How many choices does each die have if it may not show 5?
Why does the resulting 5 by 5 block contain every failure outcome exactly once?
Why would adding the 5-row and 5-column as 6+6 overcount?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Count the complete no-5 rectangle first: five choices for each die.

steps.title: Count the complete opposite
steps.body: Neither die is 5 when each die uses one of its five other faces.

steps.title: Subtract from 1
steps.body: Every outcome either has at least one 5 or has no 5.

steps.title: Another way—and its repair
steps.body: The six outcomes in the 5-row and six in the 5-column overlap at (5,5), so direct counting gives 6+6-1=11, not 12.

resolution.takeaway: A clean complement can avoid overlap; any direct count must still count each outcome exactly once.

beats.purpose: Directly repair the misconception that not exactly one means none.
beats.expectedRealization: Not exactly one head contains both zero heads and two heads, so its probability is 1-2/4=1/2.
beats.transitionIn: At least one failed in only one direction. Now use the earlier language audit on a condition that can fail by having too few or too many.
beats.transitionOut: The complement of exactly one was not just TT; it was TT together with HH.
beats.whyNow: The learner must demonstrate that complement construction, not keyword matching, controls the subtraction.
beats.entryBridge: First measure exactly one head, then let every remaining outcome form its complement.
beats.exitBridge: HT and TH make exactly one head; HH and TT make not exactly one.
learnerPrompts: Which outcomes have exactly one head?
Which remaining outcomes have zero or two heads?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Not exactly one includes both HH and TT, not only the no-head outcome.

visual.ariaLabel: Two-toss grid with HH and TT marked as not exactly one head

steps.title: Measure exactly one
steps.body: HT and TH are the two exactly-one outcomes.

steps.title: Take everything else
steps.body: HH has two heads and TT has none, so both are in the complement.

resolution.takeaway: “Not exactly one” means every count except one.

beats.purpose: Extend at-least-one reasoning to repeated four-way outcomes without a prebuilt grid.
beats.expectedRealization: No 4 on three spins has probability 27/64, so at least one 4 has probability 37/64.
beats.transitionIn: The dice grid was visible. Now build the size of a three-step complement from choices per step.
beats.transitionOut: The seven possible counts and positions of 4 were replaced by one uniform no-4 calculation.
beats.whyNow: The learner transfers the complement rule from a visible grid to multiplicative sample-space counting.
beats.entryBridge: For the complement, each spin may land on 1, 2, or 3 but not 4.
beats.exitBridge: There are 27 no-4 sequences among 64 total sequences, leaving 37 favorable sequences.
learnerPrompts: How many total three-spin sequences are possible?
How many choices remain on each spin when 4 is forbidden?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Count the no-4 sequences: three allowed results on each of three spins.

steps.title: Count all equally likely sequences
steps.body: Four results are possible on each of three spins.

steps.title: Count the complete opposite
steps.body: With no 4, each spin has only 1, 2, or 3.

steps.title: Subtract probabilities
steps.body: The 27 no-4 sequences are exactly the complement.

resolution.takeaway: Repeated at-least-one events often become repeated none-of-that-event choices.

beats.purpose: Challenge the learner to recognize all-distinct as the simple complement of at least one repeated result.
beats.expectedRealization: Three four-sided rolls have a repeat unless all three are distinct, giving 1-(4·3·2)/4^3=5/8.
beats.transitionIn: One last event has many overlapping success shapes: the first two can match, the last two can match, or all three can match. Search for the clean other side.
beats.transitionOut: All-distinct counted the complete complement without separating overlapping repeat cases.
beats.whyNow: This challenge requires discovering a useful complement rather than responding to the phrase at least one alone.
beats.entryBridge: Negate “at least one repeated result” as “all three results are distinct.”
beats.exitBridge: Twenty-four all-distinct sequences leave forty repeat sequences among sixty-four total.
learnerPrompts: What must be true if no result repeats?
After the first result, how many choices keep the second and third results distinct?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Count the complement: four choices, then three different choices, then two still-unused choices.

steps.title: Name the clean opposite
steps.body: No repeated result means all three results are distinct.

steps.title: Count all-distinct sequences
steps.body: Choose any first result, then avoid it, then avoid both earlier results.

steps.title: Subtract from the whole
steps.body: There are 4^3=64 total sequences.

resolution.takeaway: When success cases overlap, their all-distinct or none counterpart may be a single clean product.

beats.purpose: Consolidate the complete complementary-probability routine and its language checks before opening a forward question.
beats.expectedRealization: Reliable complementary probability requires an exact opposite, a partition audit, an easier calculation, and subtraction from 1.
beats.transitionIn: Traffic lights, cards, coins, dice, and spinners all used the same reasoning. Gather the checks that made every subtraction legal.
beats.prompt: Which checks belong in a reliable complementary-probability plan? Select all four.

options.text: Name every way the target event can fail.
Verify the event and its complement cover everything with no overlap.
Use the complement only when it is easier to measure.

response.feedback: Each statement protects a different part of the method.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes—exact opposite, partition, strategic choice, then subtraction from 1.
beats.incorrectFeedback: All four checks matter: define, audit, choose, and subtract.

steps.title: Protect the subtraction
steps.body: A missing failure case or an overlapping case means the two probabilities will not form the whole 1.

steps.title: Keep the strategy optional
steps.body: Complementary probability is powerful when the other side is simpler, not because every probability needs subtraction.

resolution.takeaway: Find the exact other side, prove the two sides make the whole, then use P(event)=1-P(complement).

beats.purpose: Create an unresolved transfer question only after the core method has been consolidated.
beats.expectedRealization: Some probability questions may involve two named events that are neither complements nor disjoint, so overlap must be handled explicitly.
beats.transitionIn: The complement audit is secure. Now loosen one condition: suppose two events do not form exact opposite sides.
beats.prompt: If one event is “the first die is even” and another is “the sum is even,” some outcomes belong to both. How should a probability method keep that overlap from being counted twice?
beats.takeaway: Complements are the cleanest two-part split. When events overlap instead, the shared region will need its own accounting.

notes: Draft connector lesson authored with the repository-local mathinking-lesson Skill and the compact P3 context packet.
The opening briefly reactivates C5's whole-minus-opposite audit, then advances by discovering that the probability whole is 1.
Complementary probability is named only after the learner partitions the traffic-light cycle and solves the approved anchor.
The approved 1999 AMC 8 Problem 10 is the visual anchor; 2001 AMC 8 Problem 18 transfers the method to a grid and shows overlap repair only after the complement solution.
All visuals reuse existing generic primitives and mapped problem animations, so no renderer or schema changes were required.
Generated answers were independently verified by enumeration plus a separate counting or algebraic check.
